newsitem.title: ZAIRE: New Zaire banknotes run into trouble.
newsitem.headline: New Zaire banknotes run into trouble.

text.p: New larger denomination Zairean banknotes have been widely rejected in the capital Kinshasa since their release last week.

But as the government and the central bank prepared to force the notes into circulation by using them to pay civil servants, members of parliament and other state creditors, critics gave a warning of devastating consequences.
Zaire's main human rights organization, AZADHO, on Wednesday called for the notes to be withdrawn, saying that their circulation risked causing a major social explosion.

The issue of new banknotes during a period of galloping inflation in 1992 led to widespread looting by soldiers after the radical opposition rejected the bills as worthless pieces of paper. Soldiers were paid in the new bills.

Any widespread trouble over the new notes would complicate a national crisis over a rebellion in eastern Zaire by Rwandan- backed rebels who seized territory while President Mobutu Sese Seko was in Europe for cancer treatment last year.
Mobutu returned to Zaire last month, reshuffled his government and military command and went back to France last week. State radio said on Wednesday he would return to Zaire in a few days.
Zairean soldiers, some of whom have not been paid for months, are pillaging towns while retreating from the east.

"Straight after the release of the notes...prices of basic commodities rose, opening the way to a hyperinflation without precedent much to the detriment of the general population," AZADHO said in a statement.
"The population is reluctant to use the notes which they fear will be the cause of an eventual social explosion."

The announcement 11 days ago that the notes, in one million, 500,000 and 100,000 zaire denominations, would be released forced a dramatic increase in the cost of basic commodities, with some foodstuffs more than doubling in price overnight.
Radical opposition parties immediately called for a total boycott, followed by union members and some leading businessmen.

On the informal "Wall Street" money market in downtown Kinshasa, the peach-coloured 100,000 new zaire bill is called "Mimi Orange" after a Zairean-made fizzy orange drink which went out of production years ago.
In part as a result of the effective boycott the zaire has in the past few days stabilised at around 160,000 to the dollar, moneychangers said on Wednesday.

"People are refusing to buy the notes. They are only circulating in a few circles here and those dealers demand half again as much to the dollar for the new notes," currency dealer Bopaul Mbwangi said.
The majority of the moneychangers are themselves refusing to deal in the bills, he added.
In Kinshasa's sprawling shantytowns and markets, pulling out the new bills can earn you broken ribs and worse.
Newspapers have reported numerous incidents in which people trying to use the bills have been beaten by angry mobs.
Supermarkets and major international hotels have joined street vendors and market traders in refusing the notes.
The Bank of Zaire (central bank) says it printed the larger notes to pay civil service salary arrears, and to keep up with the 750 percent inflation rate in 1996.
Supporters of the move say the new notes are more economical to print than the small denominations worth next to nothing.
Critics say that by normal monetary standards, Zaire's declined production rates should have made printing new money unnecessary.
The notes themselves fuel hyperinflation, penalising among others Zaire's already pauperised civil servants, they add.
